recognition.identity: UCI Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention Dataset (UCI ID 468), also identified in the supplied bundle with its 2019 introduction paper.
recognition.basis: Recognition comes from the supplied metadata; I have not independently retrieved or analyzed the dataset.

candidates.title: Does SpecialDay add a signal beyond Month?
candidates.question: After accounting for Month, session activity, and supplied traffic context, does SpecialDay provide reproducible information about Revenue?

core.object: The conditional association between SpecialDay and session-level Revenue.
core.relation_or_action: Compare identical held-out predictions from a model with Month and supplied session context against the same model adding SpecialDay.
core.contrast: Month and context alone versus those features plus SpecialDay.
core.prediction: Adding SpecialDay will modestly improve held-out log loss, indicating that its graded calendar-proximity value contains information beyond the coarse Month category.
core.independent_unit: Session, as described in the supplied metadata.

candidates.failure_condition: The added feature does not reproducibly improve held-out log loss, or its conditional association is too uncertain to distinguish from no association.
assumptions: SpecialDay is measured consistently across sessions.
The one-year data can assess within-dataset incremental association, not year-to-year stability.
An observational association does not establish that a promotion or other intervention on SpecialDay changes purchases.
candidates.required_new_data: None for the proposed within-dataset comparison; multiple years of dated sessions would be needed to assess stability across years.
candidates.domain_value: Could determine whether a graded special-day calendar signal adds information beyond month-level seasonality when evaluating session analytics.
candidates.discriminating_delta: Tests whether a calendar-proximity measure adds information conditional on Month and session context; prior candidates focused on duration composition, PageValues timing, and month-varying duration associations.

candidates.title: Does a delivery-information prompt change conversion near special days?
candidates.question: Among eligible shopping sessions near a special day, does showing a delivery-date and cutoff-time message change purchase completion compared with the site's usual page?

core.object: Purchase completion after a randomized delivery-information prompt.
core.relation_or_action: Randomize eligible sessions to receive a clear delivery-date/cutoff message or the usual experience, then compare Revenue rates.
core.contrast: Prompt shown versus usual experience among sessions eligible under a prespecified calendar rule.
core.prediction: The prompt will increase purchase completion when delivery timing is relevant to the special-day purchase window.
core.independent_unit: Eligible shopper, with assignment persisted across their sessions during the experiment.

candidates.failure_condition: The prespecified difference in purchase rates is zero or negative, or the experiment cannot maintain assignment and outcome measurement at the shopper level.
assumptions: Delivery timing is a meaningful purchase constraint for the tested products.
The prompt does not alter price or product availability.
The supplied SpecialDay field alone does not establish customer intent or intervention benefit.
candidates.required_new_data: A live randomized test with shopper-level assignment, eligibility dates, prompt exposure, and completed-purchase outcomes; compare purchase rates and report uncertainty by assigned group.
candidates.domain_value: Tests a concrete operational intervention tied to delivery timing rather than treating an observational calendar feature as a causal lever.
candidates.discriminating_delta: Introduces randomized exposure and a delivery-timing intervention, unlike the prior observational comparisons of session features.

candidates.title: Do BounceRates and ExitRates carry distinct session-level signals?
candidates.question: After accounting for page counts, recorded durations, and supplied context, does each of BounceRates and ExitRates provide distinct information about Revenue, or does one add little once the other is included?

core.object: The conditional associations of BounceRates and ExitRates with session-level Revenue.
core.relation_or_action: Compare otherwise identical held-out models using neither metric, each metric separately, and both together.
core.contrast: Incremental held-out contribution of each metric when the other and supplied session context are present.
core.prediction: The two metrics will not be fully interchangeable: at least one will retain incremental association when conditioned on the other and session activity.
core.independent_unit: Session, as described in the supplied metadata.

candidates.failure_condition: Neither metric reproducibly adds held-out information when the other and activity measures are included.
assumptions: The supplied aggregate fields correspond to the documented analytics measures.
Distinct predictive information would not establish distinct behavioral mechanisms or causal effects.
Model results may depend on functional form and overlap among session metrics.
candidates.required_new_data: None for the proposed conditional association; page-level event data and metric-generation details would be needed to validate the fields as measures of separate session processes.
candidates.domain_value: Could clarify whether two commonly used analytics fields warrant separate monitoring in session-level analyses.
candidates.discriminating_delta: Examines whether two documented analytics measures are conditionally distinct, rather than testing purchase prediction generally or duration allocation.

selection_reason: I1 is a focused comparison that the supplied rows can support. It separates graded special-day proximity from the coarser Month category and makes a falsifiable incremental-information prediction. Its result would remain observational and limited to this dataset.

task.deliverable: Using all supplied rows, compare paired held-out Revenue log loss for otherwise identical models with Month, session activity, and supplied context, with and without SpecialDay. Use session-level splits and training-only preprocessing. Report paired differences and uncertainty across repeated splits, the conditional SpecialDay association with uncertainty, and the feature definitions. Exclude PageValues from both models to avoid relying on its documented outcome-adjacent meaning.
task.acceptance: Before computation, forecast that adding SpecialDay will modestly improve held-out log loss. Use identical splits for both models and report the result whether positive, null, or negative. Treat the comparison as within-dataset observational evidence, not an intervention effect or proof of year-to-year stability. If the gain is not reproducible or the association is too uncertain to establish direction, record that I1 is not supported.
